content: 1. Adverse events associated with linezolid are significantly more frequent when the daily dosage exceeds 600 mg. The risk of serious adverse effects increases with prolonged use of linezolid. 2. Linezolid has the potential to interact with other drugs that influence serotonin levels in the body. When administered concurrently with certain drug classes, it can lead to serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition. 3. Drugs that increase serotonin levels and may result in serotonin syndrome include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine and paroxetine, tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline, serotonin 5-HT1 receptor agonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) like phenelzine and isocarboxazid, and other serotonergic agents such as meperidine, bupropion, buspirone, and quetiapine. 4. The use of drugs with overlapping toxicity or drug-drug interactions with linezolid should be avoided whenever possible. However, in cases where no alternative options exist, the potential benefits of using linezolid may outweigh the risks. 5. Clofazimine, an anti-leprosy drug with in vitro activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, has been used as a second-line TB medication for years. Evidence supports its effectiveness and safety, but it may cause additive QT prolongation when combined with other drugs like bedaquiline or delamanid. ECG monitoring is recommended in such cases. 6. Common side effects of clofazimine include reversible orange or red discoloration of the skin, conjunctiva, cornea, and body fluids, as well as dry skin, pruritus, rash, ichthyosis, and photosensitivity. Patients should be informed about these reversible changes to alleviate concerns. 7. Clofazimine is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding due to limited data and potential pigmentation of the infant. Dose adjustments may be necessary in patients with severe hepatic insufficiency. 8. Cycloserine, a bacteriostatic drug that inhibits cell wall synthesis, has no known cross-resistance with other TB drugs. Terizidone, composed of two cycloserine molecules, can be used interchangeably with cycloserine. 9. Cycloserine and terizidone should only be considered when other criteria for effectiveness are met, as reliable drug susceptibility testing (DST) is not available for these drugs. Patients should be informed about potential adverse effects, including central nervous system (CNS) toxicity, which may manifest as difficulty concentrating, lethargy, seizures, depression, psychosis, or suicidal ideation. 10. Peripheral neuropathy and skin reactions, such as lichen planus-like eruptions or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, are other possible side effects of cycloserine. Its use during pregnancy is not well-studied but may be considered if no better options exist. 11. Group C drugs, including ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, ethionamide/prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid, are lower-priority agents due to reduced efficacy or higher toxicity. They are included in longer regimens when Group A and B agents are insufficient. 12. Ethambutol, a first-line TB drug, has a good safety profile at recommended dosages and may be added to longer MDR-TB regimens. 13. Delamanid is recommended for use in adults and children aged 3 years or older as a Group C agent. Evidence supports its use for up to 6 months, but longer durations may be considered on a case-by-case basis. 14. Combining bedaquiline and delamanid may result in additive QT prolongation, but no severe QT prolongation was observed in a randomized controlled trial. 15. Pyrazinamide is recommended in longer regimens only when DST confirms susceptibility. Otherwise, it is not counted as an effective drug. 16. Carbapenems, such as imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem, are administered intravenously and are effective in MDR-TB regimens. However, their use is limited by the need for daily IV administration and resource constraints. 17. Amikacin and streptomycin are injectable aminoglycosides recommended only when oral agents are insufficient, susceptibility is demonstrated, and monitoring for adverse events is in place. Amikacin is preferred over streptomycin due to lower resistance rates. 18. Injectable agents should be used cautiously in children due to the risk of hearing loss, which can impact language development and learning. Their use should be limited to salvage therapy under strict monitoring. 19. Ethionamide and prothionamide are interchangeable and may be used when other effective agents are unavailable. 20. p-Aminosalicylic acid (PAS) is considered a last-resort treatment for MDR/RR-TB when better options are not available. It has no cross-resistance with other anti-TB drugs. 21. High-dose isoniazid (10–15 mg/kg) is not commonly used in longer MDR-TB regimens for adults but may be effective in certain cases of isolated inhA mutations. Peripheral neuropathy is a common side effect, and pyridoxine supplementation is recommended. 22. Kanamycin and capreomycin are no longer recommended due to increased risks of treatment failure, relapse, and death, as well as significant toxicities, including permanent hearing and kidney damage. 23. The selection of agents for longer MDR-TB regimens follows a stepwise approach based on the latest WHO guidelines, prioritizing efficacy and safety.
